decision: I used drop_duplicates() to remove the exact duplicate rows, keeping the first copy. There did not seem to be a reason to keep identical rows more than once.
reason: There were 45 rows that were exact copies of another registry row. Keeping these would probably end up counting the same patients more than once, so I removed them. This left 30000 patients, with one row per patient_id.

issue: gender spellings that are not a code
decision: I stripped the spaces and made the gender values lowercase before mapping the different spellings to F, M, or X using a dictionary. Anything that did not match was left missing, along with the blank values, and I stored the column as a category.
reason: There were 6968 gender values that were not written as F, M, or X, mostly things like woman, Male, or nb, along with 486 blank values. I was not really sure how to handle these without making assumptions about what they meant, so I left them missing rather than creating another code. This left 863 patients with missing gender values.

decision: I made the site codes uppercase and removed the hyphens and spaces so they would match the other files more easily. I left E04 as it was since that is how it was recorded in the registry.
reason: I found 1811 site codes written in different ways, such as n-01, N 01, or s02. These could cause issues when joining with sites.csv because the same site might end up being treated as multiple different sites. E04 was kept since it was the code recorded for 555 patients, and I did not want to change it without a reason.

decision: I changed the 9999 values to missing and stored birth_year as Int64, since 9999 seemed to be used as a placeholder for years that were not recorded.
reason: There were 371 patients with birth_year recorded as 9999, which seemed to mean that the year was not recorded. Leaving these values as numbers would make the maximum birth year 9999, which would obviously cause problems if I tried to calculate age.

issue: weight column named wt_kg in visits_south.csv
decision: I renamed wt_kg to weight_kg in a copy of the south file before combining the two visit files. This seemed like the simplest way to keep the weights in one column.
reason: The south office used wt_kg instead of weight_kg for the weight column. Without renaming it, stacking the files would probably leave me with two separate weight columns, so I changed the name before combining them. This gave me one weight_kg column across all 57371 visit rows.

issue: sbp sentinel 999 and readings outside 70 through 250
decision: I changed the 999 values and readings below 70 or above 250 to missing, but kept the visits themselves. I figured it was better to leave the other information intact rather than remove the entire row. Values of exactly 70 and 250 were kept since they are still within the range.
reason: There were 341 readings recorded as 999, which seemed to be the code for a measurement that was not taken, and another 116 readings outside the 70 to 250 range. These did not seem like valid blood pressure readings, but the rest of the visit was still usable. I only made the SBP values missing and kept exactly 70 and 250 since the range is inclusive.

issue: impossible and loosely written visit dates
decision: I kept visit_date only when it was written exactly as YYYY-MM-DD and represented a real calendar date. The other values were changed to missing, but I kept the rest of the visit since that information could still be useful.
reason: I found 169 dates that were either impossible or written in a different format, such as 2026-2-10 or 2026/01/22. I was not comfortable guessing what the intended date was since that could put the visit on the wrong day. The rest of the visit information was still usable, so I only changed the date to missing.

decision: I sorted by visit_time and used drop_duplicates() with keep='last' to keep the later reading for each patient_id and visit pair. These seemed to be rechecks from the same visit, so keeping the later one made the most sense to me.
reason: After removing the exact duplicates, there were still 120 visits with two readings taken minutes apart. These looked like rechecks from the same visit, so I kept the later reading to get one row per patient_id and visit. This should also make the pivot and one-to-one A1c join work properly.

decision: I kept the current record for each site_code in sites_current and left out the retired records. This seemed like the best way to avoid having multiple records for the same site when joining the data.
reason: N01 and S02 each had a current and a retired record in sites.csv. Joining all of these would probably duplicate the visits for those sites, so I kept only the current records. This gave me one site name per site_code and removed the 2 retired rows.
